Name: The Go Memory Model
Downloadable / offline docs: Single HTML page; ships inside the Go source tree
Notes: Defines happens-before for Go. Updated in 2022 to make atomics sequentially consistent — pre-2022 summaries of it are wrong. Read before arguing about channels versus mutexes.

Name: sync
Downloadable / offline docs: go doc sync; full godoc available offline via pkgsite
Notes: Mutex, RWMutex, WaitGroup, Once, Cond, Pool, Map. Small enough that reading the source is a rite of passage.

Name: sync/atomic
Notes: Compare-and-swap plus the typed atomics added in Go 1.19. The package doc's happens-before paragraph is the practical summary of the memory model.

Name: Data Race Detector
Notes: go test -race — built on ThreadSanitizer. Background in the race-detector blog post (https://go.dev/blog/race-detector).

Name: Channels & select (Tour + spec)
Notes: The spec's channel section is short and precise: a send happens before the corresponding receive completes. Most channel folklore reduces to one sentence.

Name: context
Notes: Cancellation and deadlines as a first-class value. Misusing it (storing it in long-lived structs) is a reliable interview conversation.

Name: errgroup
Notes: WaitGroup plus error propagation plus context cancellation in about a hundred lines. Read it once WaitGroup makes sense.

Name: java.util.concurrent
Notes: Executors, BlockingQueue, ConcurrentHashMap, Future. The package javadoc reads like a textbook; it is better than almost every blog post written about it.

Name: java.util.concurrent.atomic
Notes: CAS-based counters/accumulators and field updaters; the javadoc states the memory effects of every method.

Name: java.util.concurrent.locks
Notes: Lock, ReadWriteLock, Condition and AbstractQueuedSynchronizer. AQS is the framework behind most of j.u.c; its javadoc is the deep end worth reaching.

Name: CompletableFuture
Notes: Composable futures behind an awkward API. The completion-ordering and default-executor rules in the javadoc are worth reading in full.

Name: JLS chapter 17 — Threads and Locks
Notes: The normative Java Memory Model. Volatile, monitors and final-field semantics stated as rules, not folklore. All spec versions live one level up.

Name: JCStress
Notes: The JVM litmus-test harness from OpenJDK. If you believe something about the JMM/ prove it here.

Name: JMH
Notes: The JVM benchmark harness. Concurrency benchmarks are where naive measurement dies; JMH exists because of that.

Name: Virtual threads (JEP 444)
Notes: Finalized in JDK 21. Millions of blocked threads on a small pool of carriers — with the pinning caveat around synchronized that everyone should be able to explain.

Name: Structured concurrency (JEP 505)
Notes: Fifth preview (JDK 25). Threads with a lifetime: a failure cancels the siblings. Long lineage — JEP 428/ 437/ 453/ 480/ 499/ then this.

Name: Scoped values (JEP 506)
Notes: Finalized in JDK 25. The immutable successor to ThreadLocal, designed for virtual threads.

Name: std::sync
Notes: Mutex, RwLock, Arc, mpsc, Barrier, Condvar. The Send and Sync traits (in std::marker) are the actual concurrency-safety mechanism; the module docs say so plainly.

Name: std::sync::atomic
Notes: Atomics with explicit orderings. The module documentation is a miniature memory-model course in itself.

Name: Tokio
Notes: The dominant async runtime: scheduler/ timers/ IO. Know the contract — std provides the primitives/ Tokio schedules them — and you can answer the async-runtime-from-scratch interview question.

Name: Asynchronous Programming in Rust (the async book)
Notes: Why futures are lazy/ what pinning is for/ and what the compiler actually builds out of async/await.

Name: The Rustonomicon
Notes: Its chapter on Send/Sync and data races is the most precise public statement of Rust's concurrency guarantees. The unsafe-code book overall.

Name: Loom
Notes: Exhaustive model checker for concurrent Rust under the C11 memory model. Slow and thorough — use it on primitives/ not applications.

Name: Miri
Notes: An interpreter that detects undefined behaviour, including some data races. Complements Loom: UB detection versus interleaving exploration.

Name: crossbeam
Notes: Epoch-based reclamation, scoped threads, channels and deques. The engineering that made non-blocking Rust practical.

Name: parking_lot
Notes: Faster, smaller replacements for std::sync primitives. Reading why it exists teaches you what std's portability constraints actually are.

Name: Rust Atomics and Locks — Mara Bos
Downloadable / offline docs: Free and complete online; print editions exist
Notes: Written by a Rust library team lead. The clearest treatment of memory ordering in any language, free — do not let Rust in the title scare you off if you write C++ or Java.

Name: C++ memory model
Notes: The happens-before formalism that every other language borrowed. cppreference 403s automated clients; fine in a browser.

Name: std::atomic
Notes: Per-operation orderings/ the is_lock_free honesty check/ and std::atomic_ref for shared buffers.

Name: C++ thread support library
Notes: std::thread, jthread, mutexes, condition variables, futures, latches and barriers — the standard library sitting on top of the memory model.

Name: C11 atomics (`stdatomic.h`)
Notes: C11 adopted the same memory model with a much smaller library. Useful reminder that the model/ not the API/ is the important part.

Name: P2300 — std::execution
Notes: Senders and receivers — the standard C++ async framework adopted for C++26. Structured, dependency-aware, allocation-conscious.

Name: libuv
Notes: The event loop under Node.js. Handles, requests and the thread pool — the clearest production example of concurrency-is-not-parallelism in C.

Name: Folly
Notes: Futures, AtomicHashMap, MPMCQueue and friends — battle-tested at Meta scale. Reading it is a graduate course in applied lock-free engineering.

Name: ThreadSanitizer
Notes: Happens-before tracking at runtime/ in C/C++ and Go. Understand its false negatives before trusting a clean run.

Name: Valgrind — Helgrind & DRD
Notes: Two independent race detectors in one manual — Helgrind (happens-before) and DRD (lockset). Slower but sometimes deeper than TSan.

Name: oneTBB
Notes: Intel's Threading Building Blocks: work-stealing task arenas, flow graphs, concurrent containers. The reference design for task-based C++ parallelism.

Name: .NET Task Parallel Library
Notes: Task, Parallel.For, PLINQ — data parallelism documentation that explains its own scheduling instead of hiding it.

Name: System.Threading.Channels
Notes: The producer/consumer primitive behind modern .NET async pipelines. Bounded and unbounded/ with backpressure semantics documented.

Name: Python — threading
Notes: Shared-memory threads under the GIL: bytecode-level serialization/ lock ordering traps. Pair with the GIL chapter of this book.

Name: Python — asyncio
Notes: Event loop, coroutines, Tasks, the executor bridge. The docs are unusually candid about what runs where.

Name: PEP 703 — free-threaded CPython
Notes: Removing the GIL. Optional build in 3.13/ officially supported in 3.14 — watch a language grow a real memory model in public.

Name: Erlang/OTP
Notes: Processes, message passing, supervision, links and monitors. For the scheduler itself the canonical references are the OTP efficiency guide and Erik Stenman's The BEAM Book — name-only. Preemption in small reductions is why no process can starve its neighbours.

Name: Elixir — Task & GenServer
Notes: Task for one-shot async/ GenServer for stateful servers — the actor pattern with supervision trees spelled out.

Name: Kotlin coroutines
Notes: Structured concurrency as a language feature: Job hierarchies/ cancellation as cooperation/ dispatchers as schedulers.

Name: Akka (and Apache Pekko)
SDKs & notable repos: Apache Pekko — https://pekko.apache.org/ — the open-source fork created after Akka's 2022 license change
Notes: The industrial-strength actor toolkit: clustering, persistence, streams. Check which of the two your employer can actually use.

Name: Microsoft Orleans
Notes: Virtual actors — grains are activated on demand and single-threaded per identity. The most honest documentation of actor placement and lifecycle anywhere.

Name: Clojure — concurrency reference
Notes: atoms, refs (STM), agents, vars — a language that shipped an opinionated concurrency taxonomy instead of one mechanism.

Name: moodycamel::ConcurrentQueue
Notes: Single-header lock-free MPMC queue/ widely adopted in game engines and audio. The README doubles as a design document.

Name: liburcu
Notes: Userspace RCU — QSBR flavors/ defer-reclaim/ call-RCU. Pairs directly with the kernel RCU documentation below.

Name: JCTools
Notes: SPSC/MPSC/MPMC Java queues used by Netty and RxJava. The JMH benchmarks inside are the real tutorial.

Name: Vyukov bounded MPMC queue
Notes: The bounded multi-producer/multi-consumer queue everyone copies — fixed-size cells/ sequence numbers/ one CAS per operation.

Name: 1024cores.net
SDKs & notable repos: Dmitry Vyukov's collection of scalable algorithms — bounded MPMC/ rolling queue/ lazy stack/ the original work-stealing write-ups
Notes: The historical reference for this entire field/ and frequently unreachable; the content survives in mirrors and the Wayback Machine.

Name: crossbeam-epoch
SDKs & notable repos: The epoch module of the crossbeam repository
Notes: Epoch-based reclamation: how lock-free structures free memory without a garbage collector. Read with hazard pointers for contrast.

Name: seqlock (kernel docs)
Notes: Sequence counters: writers bump a sequence/ readers retry on odd counts. The classic optimistic-read pattern/ with its writer-starvation caveats stated.

Name: RCU (kernel docs)
Notes: Read-copy-update — the answer to how the kernel reads shared data without taking a lock. Start with the What-is-RCU document; it rewards patience.

Name: TLA+
Notes: Lamport's specification language: concurrency as mathematics, with TLC exhausting the reachable states. The video course on the same page is the gentlest entry.

Name: TLA+ tools
Notes: The TLC model checker, the Toolbox IDE and the community modules, all open source.

Name: PlusCal
Notes: An algorithm language that compiles to TLA+. Start here; drop to raw TLA+ only when PlusCal cannot say what you mean.

Name: GenMC
Notes: Model checking for C programs under the C11 memory model — the research tool behind a line of PPoPP/PLDI papers. The Rust analogues are Loom and Miri.

Name: Shuttle
Notes: AWS's randomized scheduler for Rust tests: bounded/ seedable exploration of interleavings that unit tests never see.

Name: CDSChecker
Notes: Memory-model-aware model checking for C11 (SOSP 2013). Where the C11-is-weaker-than-you-think results came from.

Name: async-profiler
Notes: Low-overhead sampling for the JVM. Wall-clock mode makes lock waits and IO waits visible where a CPU profiler shows nothing.

Name: jcmd & jstack
Notes: Thread dumps remain the fastest path from the-server-is-stuck to which-monitor. jcmd Thread.print subsumes jstack.

Name: Go pprof
Notes: One import to a profiling endpoint. Goroutine dumps find leaks/ and the block and mutex profiles surface contention directly.

Name: Java Flight Recorder & Mission Control
Notes: Always-on flight recording shipped in the JDK since 11; JMC is the viewer. Production-safe enough to leave enabled.

Name: Eclipse MAT
Notes: Heap-dump analyzer. Its dominator tree is how you find the object (and the thread holding its monitor) that everything is waiting on.

Name: perf
Notes: perf sched and perf lock record contention from the kernel's point of view; the CPU profile catches spin-waiting that lock reports miss.

Name: OSTEP — Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces
Notes: Part II is *Concurrency*: threads, locks, condition variables, semaphores, common bugs. Free, complete, better written than the paid alternatives.

Name: The Little Book of Semaphores
Notes: Free PDF that teaches synchronization through progressively harder classical problems. greenteapress.com did not answer automated checkers at verification time; it loads in a browser and the PDF is mirrored on many university course pages.

Name: Is Parallel Programming Hard, And, If So, What Can You Do About It?
Notes: Paul McKenney's free book, continuously updated. The RCU chapters alone justify it.

Name: Rust Atomics and Locks
Notes: Free online. The clearest memory-ordering course in any language.

Name: The Rust Book — Fearless Concurrency
Notes: The shortest honest introduction to Send/Sync and message passing versus shared state.

Name: Go Concurrency Patterns: Pipelines and cancellation
Notes: The canonical staged-pipeline pattern, with cancellation done right.

Name: Go Concurrency Patterns: Context
Notes: Why cancellation belongs in a function parameter.

Name: Concurrency Is Not Parallelism (talk)
Notes: Rob Pike's talk that fixed the vocabulary. The slide deck has survived every runtime change since.

Name: Effective Go — concurrency sections
Notes: Share by communicating, goroutines, channels, select.

Name: Go by Example
Notes: Goroutines, channels, tickers, worker pools as runnable snippets. Excellent for a first pass.

Name: Oracle Java tutorial — Concurrency
Notes: The official trail: threads, synchronization, liveness hazards, executor basics.

Name: .NET — Managed threading
Notes: The conceptual overview behind the TPL: threads vs tasks, sync primitives, cancellation.

Name: Elixir — Getting Started guide
Notes: Processes and message passing introduced without ceremony.

Name: Learn You Some Erlang
Notes: The free Erlang book. The concurrency chapter is the best low-mathematics introduction to the actor model.

Name: Node.js — The event loop, timers, and nextTick
Notes: Single-threaded concurrency explained precisely by its most famous implementation.

Name: LLNL — POSIX Threads Programming
SDKs & notable repos: Tutorial classics that outlived every redesign
Notes: The pthreads tutorial that has survived every platform transition since the 1990s.

Name: LLNL — Introduction to Parallel Computing
SDKs & notable repos: Tutorial classics that outlived every redesign
Notes: Amdahl, granularity, shared vs distributed memory, in tutorial form.

Name: Python — concurrent.futures
SDKs & notable repos: Tutorial classics that outlived every redesign
Notes: Thread and process pools behind one interface. The gentlest real API in this list.

Name: P. J. Birrell, *An Introduction to Programming with Threads* (1989)
SDKs & notable repos: The classics — name-only where the PDF floats
Notes: The DEC-SRC monograph that defined threads-as-an-API. No official stable link; every systems course hosts a copy.

Name: Simon Marlow, *Parallel and Concurrent Programming in Haskell*
SDKs & notable repos: The classics — name-only where the PDF floats
Notes: Free from the author under O'Reilly's open terms; the URL has moved more than once, so search the title plus the author's site.

Name: Brian Goetz, *Java theory and practice* article series
SDKs & notable repos: The classics — name-only where the PDF floats
Notes: The pre-JCiP articles ("A brief history of the Java Memory Model" among them) remain the friendliest JMM introduction. Archived across IBM developerWorks mirrors.

Name: Herb Sutter, *The Free Lunch Is Over* (2005)
SDKs & notable repos: The classics — name-only where the PDF floats
Notes: The essay that predicted the concurrency turn. Short, dated only in its optimism about hardware clock speeds.

Name: Julia Evans — concurrency & networking zines
SDKs & notable repos: The classics — name-only where the PDF floats
Notes: Sketch-first introductions that make race conditions and queues feel small. Buy or browse at wizardzines.com.

Name: Hewitt, Bishop & Steiger, *A Universal Modular ACTOR Formalism* (1973)
SDKs & notable repos: The classics — name-only where the PDF floats
Notes: The paper that started the actor model. Paywalled at the publisher; free copies circulate from course pages.

Name: MIT 6.172 — Performance Engineering of Software Systems
SDKs & notable repos: University courses with full public materials
Notes: Lectures, labs and readings on multicore performance, all public. The C++ optimization ladder is the useful part.

Name: CMU 15-418 — Parallel Computer Architecture and Programming
SDKs & notable repos: University courses with full public materials
Notes: The best public course on why parallel programs are slow: coherence, consistency, synchronization costs.

Name: Berkeley CS267 — Applications of Parallel Computers
SDKs & notable repos: University courses with full public materials
Notes: Decades of public lecture notes on parallel algorithms. Berkeley blocks some automated clients; it loads in a browser.

Name: Herlihy, Shavit, Luchangco & Spear, *The Art of Multiprocessor Programming*
Notes: The textbook for this entire index. Concurrent objects, spin locks, queues, STM — with exercises worth doing.

Name: Goetz et al., *Java Concurrency in Practice*
Notes: Twenty years old and still the best applied book on shared-state concurrency in any managed language.

Name: Anthony Williams, *C++ Concurrency in Action*
Notes: The standard C++11 concurrency book, kept current through C++20 features.

Name: David Butenhof, *Programming with POSIX Threads*
Notes: The 1997 original; the correctness discipline has not been improved on.

Name: C. A. R. Hoare, *Communicating Sequential Processes*
Notes: The 1985 book, free PDF at usingcsp.com (site intermittently offline; widely mirrored). The algebra behind CSP, occam, Go channels and Elixir.

Name: Matt Kline — What Every Systems Programmer Should Know About Concurrency (PDF)
Notes: Free, hardware-first, the best bridge from OSTEP to the memory-model literature. The asset host 403s some automated clients; it loads in a browser.

Name: Ulrich Drepper — What Every Programmer Should Know About Memory (PDF)
Notes: Long, but the cache-coherence and NUMA background everything else assumes.

Name: Paul McKenney — *Memory Barriers: a Hardware View for Software Hackers*
Notes: No stable link; now folded into the perfbook above, with the original PDF circulating from his site.

Name: Sarita Adve & Kourosh Gharachorloo — *Shared Memory Consistency Models: A Tutorial*
Notes: The 1996 tutorial that defined how to talk about consistency. Free copies circulate from the authors' pages.

Name: Hans-J. Boehm — *Threads Cannot Be Implemented as a Library* (2005)
Notes: Why C++ needed a memory model, in one paper. Free via SIGPLAN's author-hosted copies.

Name: The JSR-133 Cookbook
Notes: Doug Lea's implementer's-eye view of the JMM: barriers for every compiler transformation.

Name: Bill Pugh — The Java Memory Model (JSR-133 FAQ)
Notes: The original JMM explainer, still the friendliest correct one.

Name: Alexey Shipilev — *Java Memory Model Pragmatics* (talk)
Notes: No official stable link; search the title. The talk that made the JMM's compiler-side consequences legible.

Name: Preshing on Programming
Notes: Jeff Preshing's posts on memory reordering and lock-free patterns are the standard reference-by-example.

Name: Mechanical Sympathy
Notes: Martin Thompson's blog; the origin of the term every low-latency team now uses.

Name: Nitsan Wakart's blog
Notes: JMH methodology, false sharing, the Java-level cost model. Dormant, still essential.

Name: The LMAX Disruptor technical paper
Notes: The design write-up behind the [LMAX-Exchange/disruptor](https://github.com/LMAX-Exchange/disruptor) repo. Ring buffers, memory barriers and the business-logic-in-6ms argument.

Name: Agner Fog — Software optimization resources
Notes: Instruction costs and microarchitecture detail; also listed in the computer-architecture index, because the hardware does not care which conference you came from.

Name: Bryan Cantrill's conference talks
Notes: No single canonical index; search "Bryan Cantrill concurrency" and "observability". The argumentation about what concurrency bugs cost is unmatched.

Name: Martin Thompson — *How WRONG is your queue?* (talk)
Notes: No official stable link; search the title. Every concurrent queue in JVM land, measured.

Name: futex(2)
Notes: What a mutex actually is on Linux. Read once; every managed runtime makes sudden sense.

Name: pthreads(7)
Notes: The overview page: thread groups, signals, NPTL. The underused companion to every pthreads tutorial.

Name: POSIX / Single UNIX Specification
Notes: pthread_create, pthread_mutex, semaphores, memory visibility — the normative floor under everything above. Also listed in the operating-systems index.

Name: Doug Lea's concurrency pages
Notes: The author of j.u.c on why it is shaped the way it is. Sparse pages, dense information.

Name: OpenMP — specifications
Notes: The pragmatic shared-memory standard: pragmas, tasking, offload. Read the 5.x spec's tasking chapter before dismissing it.

Name: OpenCilk
Notes: MIT's Cilk fork: fork-join parallelism with a provable work-stealing scheduler and a real compiler implementation.

Name: HPX
Notes: A C++ runtime for distributed task-based parallelism; the research continuum made installable.

Name: Coz
Notes: The causal profiler: tells you which line of code is worth optimizing for *latency of others*, not CPU share.

Name: rr
Notes: Record-and-replay debugging. Concurrency bugs stop being heisenbugs when every run is bit-identical.

Name: Brendan Gregg's site
Notes: Also in the operating-systems index; the off-CPU time and flame-graph material is directly about where concurrency hides time.

Name: Vyukov — *Scalable Go scheduler design doc* (2012)
Notes: No official stable link; search the title plus "Vyukov". The design note behind Go's work-stealing scheduler and half of every runtime interview question.

Name: CppCon
Notes: The C++ conference — where the memory-model and atomics talks live.

Name: NVIDIA Developer
Notes: GTC talks on GPU architecture and parallel programming; primary for accelerator design.

Name: Strange Loop Conference
Notes: The Strange Loop channel: distributed systems, databases and language talks from the conference.

Name: USENIX
Notes: Conference recordings for most USENIX papers — free video, the fastest route into a systems paper.

Name: Computerphile
Notes: Short, well-made explainers; the right first stop before a spec.

Name: InfoQ
Notes: Conference keynotes and architecture talks — good for orientation, verify specifics elsewhere.

Name: Google TechTalks
Notes: Concurrency and runtime talks, including historic ones from the authors of Go and Java libraries.

Name: Linux Plumbers Conference
Notes: Kernel scheduler, locking and memory-ordering tracks.

Name: UC Berkeley CS162 — Operating Systems (Fall 2020)
Notes: The concurrency third of this course (lectures 6–12) is the clearest free treatment of locks, semaphores and monitors.

Name: Linux Plumbers Conference
Notes: Scheduler, locking and memory-ordering microconferences — kernel concurrency discussed by the people maintaining it.

Name: USENIX ATC '26
Notes: The applied venue, open.

Name: FOSDEM video archive
Notes: Kernel and runtime devrooms.

Name: No official channel for PPoPP or SPAA
Notes: Checked on 2026-10-09; the parallel-computing conferences do not publish video. Use the ACM DL and author pages.
